title: CN-lab-03.2: Connect Network NS to Root
markdown:
# CN-lab-03.2: Connect Network NS to Root (Part 2 — Validating & Troubleshooting)

In Part 1, you added a default route to `app-ns` and proved it worked with `ip route get`. That is the easy half of the job. The harder, more valuable skill is what you do when a route like this stops working — because in production, it will, usually at the worst possible time. A route gets deleted by an automation script gone wrong, a config management tool reverts a change, someone fat-fingers an `ip route del`. The engineers who stay calm are the ones who already know, from practice, exactly what a missing default route looks like and how to confirm the fix.

This lab rebuilds the same setup from Part 1 (quickly — you've done it twice now), then deliberately breaks the default route, confirms the exact failure it causes, and restores it. By the end you will have run the full diagnostic loop once, on purpose, in a namespace where nothing real is at stake.

By the end of this lab, you will be able to:

- Inspect the ARP/neighbour cache that traffic through a gateway actually populates
- Deliberately remove a default route and confirm, precisely, what breaks
- Distinguish "the destination doesn't exist" from "there's no route to get there" — they look similar from the outside but are different problems
- Restore a deleted route and verify the fix the same way you verified the original setup

## Part 1: Rebuilding app-ns (Recap)

Same namespace, same addressing as Part 1 of this lab pair:

```bash
sudo ip netns add app-ns
sudo ip link add veth-root type veth peer name veth-app
sudo ip link set veth-app netns app-ns
sudo ip link set veth-root up
sudo ip netns exec app-ns ip link set lo up
sudo ip netns exec app-ns ip link set veth-app up
sudo ip addr add 10.30.0.1/24 dev veth-root
sudo ip netns exec app-ns ip addr add 10.30.0.2/24 dev veth-app
sudo ip netns exec app-ns ip route add default via 10.30.0.1
```

Confirm the route is there before moving on:

```bash
sudo ip netns exec app-ns ip route show
```

You should see both the directly-connected `10.30.0.0/24` entry and `default via 10.30.0.1 dev veth-app`.

## Part 2: What the Default Route Actually Populates — the ARP Cache

Before breaking anything, look at what a *working* gateway path leaves behind. Ping the gateway directly:

```bash
sudo ip netns exec app-ns ping -c 2 10.30.0.1
```

Now check the namespace's ARP/neighbour cache:

```bash
sudo ip netns exec app-ns ip neigh show
```

You will see an entry for `10.30.0.1` — the kernel resolved its MAC address the moment it needed to send a frame there. This is worth being precise about: **ARP resolves the next hop, not the final destination.** When traffic leaves through a gateway, the kernel only ever needs the gateway's own MAC address on the local link — what happens after that is the gateway's problem, not app-ns's. This is why `ip neigh show` inside a namespace with a working default route will show entries for its gateway, never for far-away destinations reached through it.

**Why it matters**: when you're debugging "I can't reach X" on a real host, `ip neigh show` tells you whether the *local* hop is resolving correctly. A missing or `FAILED` entry for your own gateway means the problem is on your own subnet — before you even get to routing.

## Part 3: Breaking It On Purpose

Now, delete the default route:

```bash
sudo ip netns exec app-ns ip route del default
```

Check the routing table:

```bash
sudo ip netns exec app-ns ip route show
```

Only the directly-connected `10.30.0.0/24` entry remains. Nothing else changed — `veth-app` is still up, the address is still assigned, the gateway is still reachable directly. Only the path to *everything else* is gone.

Now try the same lookup from Part 1, to an address outside the local subnet:

```bash
sudo ip netns exec app-ns ip route get 203.0.113.5
```

This fails again, exactly as it did before the default route existed: `RTNETLINK answers: Network is unreachable`. This is the precise, reproducible signature of a missing default route — not a DNS problem, not a firewall problem, not "the server is down" — the kernel simply has no instruction for where to send the packet.

> **Diagnostic habit**: "Network is unreachable" (from the local kernel, before any packet leaves) is a different failure from a timeout (packet sent, no reply) or "Destination Host Unreachable" (a remote router said so). Learning to read which one you're looking at tells you immediately whether the problem is your own routing table or something further away.

## Part 4: Restoring and Re-verifying

Add the exact same route back:

```bash
sudo ip netns exec app-ns ip route add default via 10.30.0.1
```

Confirm it's back:

```bash
sudo ip netns exec app-ns ip route show
```

And re-run the lookup one more time to close the loop:

```bash
sudo ip netns exec app-ns ip route get 203.0.113.5
```

It succeeds again, routed via `10.30.0.1` exactly as before. Nothing about this fix was mysterious — you removed one specific entry, watched exactly what broke because of it, and added that same entry back.

**Why it matters**: this add → observe → break → confirm → restore → re-verify loop is the entire discipline of network troubleshooting, compressed into five commands. The specific tools change (sometimes it's `ip route`, sometimes `iptables`, sometimes DNS) but the loop — know the working state, reproduce the failure precisely, fix the one thing that's actually wrong, confirm with the same check that caught it — does not.

## Conclusion

In this lab, you validated and troubleshot a default route end to end:

- `ip neigh show` after a successful gateway ping reveals the ARP entry for the *gateway itself* — ARP resolves the next hop, never the far-end destination
- Deleting a default route leaves directly-connected routes untouched — only destinations that depended on the catch-all entry stop being reachable
- `RTNETLINK answers: Network is unreachable` is the specific, reproducible signature of "the kernel has no route for this at all" — distinct from a timeout or a remote rejection
- Restoring a deleted route and re-running the same verification you used to confirm it originally is the complete diagnostic loop, and it is the same loop you will run on real infrastructure
